On Jul 22, 2014, at 9:48 PM, Alp Kucukelbir <a...@cs.columbia.edu> wrote:

> I'm making progress! Faster than I had thought, actually.

Great news.

> I have three (direct) questions for you guys and one favor to ask:
>
> [Question 1:] When I do
>
> stan::model::gradient(model_, cont_params_, log_prob, init_grad, &std::cout);
>
> versus
>
> log_prob = model_.template log_prob<false, true>(cont_params_, &std::cout);
>
> I get slightly different (yet close) numerical values for log_prob.
>
> Is there a numerical difference between the two methods? Or am I missing the Jacobian somewhere?

The three template parameters for log_prob are:

propto (boolean) whether to drop constant terms
jacobian: (boolean) whether to include the Jacobian
T: (scalar) type of scalars (stan::agrad::var, double, etc.)

The last one will be inferred automatically based on the argument

The gradient method sets both booleans to true.

We need to get the model concept better documented. The current
doc is here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Model-Concept

Please update as you find errors. For instance, I just noticed the
scalar type parameter T is in the wrong order on log_prob (so
I fixed it); there's probably a lot more that's not up to date
or correct in it.

> [Question 2:] I know that I can call stan::model::gradient to get the gradient of the log prob. The Jacobian is taken care of as well.
>
> But how should I go about calculating the gradient of the log prob composed with some affine function g(params)? I have the function implemented in C++, but I suspect I'll have to do some agrad magic...
>
> Daniel had sent me this elucidating example (see attached). Should I follow that? Or is there some built in functionality for what I'm trying to accomplish already built into Stan?

Assuming I'm understanding correctly and you want to calculate

d/dparams log_prob(g(params)),

there are a bunch of ways you can do it.

I'd suggest using the functional in stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp.

Just define a new functor class

template <typename M>
struct affine_log_prob {
const M& model_;

affine_log_prob(const M& model) : model_(model) { }

template <typename T>
T operator()(Matrix<T,Dynamic,1> x) {
return model_.template log_prob<true,true>(g(params));
}
};

Then just pass an instance of affine_log_prob into the gradient
function. It's important to keep the reference to model_ so you
don't inadvertently make a copy --- model instances have all the data
instantiated.

You'll need to construct the instance with both the model (and specify
the appropriate type to the struct's template parameter) and
also whatever parameters are involved in computing g (e.g., a matrix
and vector if it's an affine transform with translation).

> [Question 3:] While I'm developing on /feature/bbvb/, I would like to "keep tabs" on what's happening on /develop. Currently I do the following
>
> (I'm working on /feature/bbvb.)
> git pull
> git merge develop
>
> But I read that I might want to be doing "rebasing" instead. What do you guys recommend?

Rebasing erases the history of your commits, which is something
different. We want to make sure all the commits at least compile so
that we can run git bisect to find problems when necessary. If they
don't, then rebasing can be used --- I don't even know how to do it.

You want to do:

> git pull origin develop

in order to merge the latest develop into your feature.

> [Favor 1:] Could one of you take a look at /feature/bbvb/ and tell me how I'm ruining all that is beautiful in Stan? I would appreciate any tips/pointers/suggestions/etc on the code.

What should I look at in that branch (feature/bbvb --- you
don't need leading/trailing slashes)?

The main thing that code needs is to not be in too quirky a style
and to pass reasonable unit tests.

- Bob

>
> which adds the normalization constants of the distributions.
>

Michael's right about what the code's doing, but this isn't how
it should be called because we don't need to compute the normalizing
constant.

The model_functional class (which should be called "model_functor")
is indeed specifying log_prob<true,true>, but it should be calling
log_prob<false,true>. At least for HMC, NUTS and optimization.
So one option if you need it to be <true,true> elsewhere is to
add two more template parameters to model_functor (assuming it
gets renamed properly).

I'm creating an issue that I think we should deal with for 2.4.0++.

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/797

> If it’s affine then you should be able to modify the gradient directly,
>
> g = a * f + b
> dg/dx = a * df/dx + b,
>
> no? In any case, if g is nonlinear then you’ll have to implement a functor.

Nice to have someone who actually understands calculus!
Michael's suggestion should be more efficient than calculating
via autodiff.

> git pull -ff origin develop to keep up with dev. You would rebase your branch before merge back into develop.

You should only rebase if the intermediate commits do not leave
Stan in a coherent state (and you probably shouldn't be doing that).

If anyone can explain how to do rebasing in a safe way, could they
put it in the developer process wiki on stan-dev/stan? I don't even
know how to do it and it looks scary.

- Bob

Alp,

Firstly, your calls to model::log_prob are inconsistent. You call model::log_prob<false, true> and model::log_prob<true, false>, but not
model::log_prob<true, true> which what gradient calls. Now you will still see a discrepancy between the log_prob you get from
gradient and the one you get from model::log_prob<true, true> because the latter treats everything as a constant, so only the
Jacobian survives. In the former only terms that don’t depend on the inputs are dropped.

Once you take this into account everything is consistent.
